title: VHS
wiki_lead:
VHS (Video Home System) is a discontinued standard for consumer-level analog video recording on tape cassettes, introduced on September 9, 1976 by the Victor Company of Japan (JVC, a subsidiary of Matsushita). It was the dominant home video format throughout the tape media period of the 1980s and 1990s.
Magnetic tape video recording was adopted by the television industry in the 1950s in the form of the first commercialized video tape recorders (VTRs), but the devices were expensive and used only in professional environments. In the 1970s, videotape technology became affordable for home use, and widespread adoption of videocassette recorders (VCRs) began; the VHS became the most popular media format for VCRs as it would win the "format war" against Betamax (backed by Sony) and a number of other competing tape standards.
The cassettes themselves use a 0.5-inch (12.7 mm) magnetic tape between two spools and typically offer a capacity of at least two hours. The popularity of VHS was intertwined with the rise of the video rental market, when films were released on pre-recorded videotapes for home viewing. Newer improved tape formats such as S-VHS were later developed, as well as the earliest optical disc format, LaserDisc; the lack of global adoption of these formats increased VHS's lifetime, which eventually peaked and started to decline in the late 1990s after the introduction of DVD, a digital optical disc format. VHS rentals were surpassed by DVD in the United States in 2003. 
Although DVD had already replaced VHS as the primary format for new releases, VHS remained common in many households due to large existing tape collections. Combo units allowed playback of both VHS tapes and DVDs in a single device and served as a transitional technology between the two formats. In addition to playback, some consumers still used VHS tapes to record television programs and home videos, although the practice was in decline. which eventually became the preferred low-end method of movie distribution. For home recording purposes, VHS and VCRs were surpassed by (typically hard disk–based) digital video recorders (DVR) in the 2000s. Production of all VHS equipment ceased by 2016, although the format has since gained some niche popularity amongst collectors and This Is How The World Ends (2026) became the first straight-to-VHS release in 20 years.

History


Before VHS

grok_lead: VHS (Video Home System) is a consumer analog video cassette recording format that uses magnetic tape housed in a plastic cassette to record and play back standard-definition video and audio signals, primarily for home use with VCRs (video cassette recorders). Developed by the Victor Company of Japan ( JVC) starting in 1971, it employs helical-scan technology on Â½-inch-wide tape to achieve up to two hours of recording time in its initial design, featuring a parallel loading mechanism, dark luminance frequency modulation (DL-FM) system for luminance signals, and a phase-shift (PS) color process to minimize interference. The format's origins trace back to JVC's efforts under engineers Shizuo Takano and Yuma Shiraishi, who established a 12-goal development matrix in 1971 to create an affordable, compact home video system amid the shift from professional U-matic formats (which used Â¾-inch tape) to consumer applications. JVC's first prototype emphasized longer recording duration over superior picture quality, leading to the release of the HR-3300 model on September 9, 1976, at a price of approximately Â¥256,000 (about $915 USD at the time), weighing 30 pounds and capable of NTSC-standard video playback. This contrasted with Sony's competing Betamax format, introduced in 1975 with the SL-6300 model offering higher resolution (around 240 lines) but limited to one-hour tapes initially, sparking the "videotape format war" where VHS ultimately prevailed due to its extended playtime, lower cost, and broader licensing to manufacturers like RCA, which brought it to the U.S. market in 1977. VHS quickly became the dominant global standard for home video, driving explosive growth in the consumer electronics industry by the early 1980s, with enhancements like the Hi-Fi stereo audio system introduced in 1983 and the higher-resolution S-VHS variant expanding its capabilities for both recording television broadcasts and distributing prerecorded movies. Its widespread adoption revolutionized entertainment, enabling time-shifting of media, home movie-making, and a boom in video rentals, while fostering advancements in magnetic tape (e.g., cobalt-alloy coatings) and integrated circuits that influenced later digital formats. By the 1990s, VHS held over 90% market share worldwide, though it was gradually supplanted by DVDs and digital streaming in the 2000s, remaining a cultural icon for analog media preservation. In recent years as of 2025, including exhibits such as "REWIND: A VHS Revival" at state fairs, VHS has seen a resurgence through nostalgia trends.
